pass_summary: GG is one of the most consumed probiotic strains in the world and is safe for the general healthy population, but a real and strain-confirmed bacteremia signal exists in specific vulnerable groups: patients with central venous catheters or other indwelling lines, immunocompromised/immunosuppressed patients (including active inflammatory bowel disease on corticosteroids), infants with short bowel syndrome, and preterm/NICU infants. All confirmed cases trace to gut mucosal translocation in a host with a compromised barrier, not to healthy oral consumption. A large ICU RCT (PROSPECT, already noted in immune.json) also found L. rhamnosus recovered from a normally sterile site at a low but significantly elevated rate versus placebo, consistent with this same risk pattern in critically ill adults.

claims.population_detail: patients with a compromised gut barrier or indwelling central line: immunocompromised/immunosuppressed patients (including active IBD on corticosteroids), short-bowel-syndrome infants, preterm/NICU infants, and critically ill adults with central venous catheters
claims.effect_size: not applicable - case reports have no denominator; genomic/molecular strain typing (WGS, PFGE, or 16S rRNA sequencing) confirmed the bloodstream isolate matched the ingested probiotic strain GG in every case cited here
claims.tier_rationale: Human safety signals of this kind live almost entirely in case reports per source policy, so tier D applies by definition regardless of how many cases exist or how tightly strain identity is confirmed. Five independent, molecularly strain-confirmed cases across four independent publications plus a strain-specific SR's safety note: (1) an immunocompetent trauma patient with a central venous catheter and GI compromise, WGS-confirmed, cleared without antibiotics; (2) an infant with short bowel syndrome, PFGE-confirmed; (3) an adult with severe active ulcerative colitis on corticosteroids, 16S-confirmed, with concurrent candidemia; (4) a pediatric ulcerative-colitis patient, 16S-confirmed, recovered after 5 days of antibiotics; (5) rare sepsis noted in preterm infants in the strain-specific NEC-prevention SR (see gi.json's gi-nec-prevention). Every identified case involves a host-side barrier or line vulnerability, not bacteremia in an otherwise healthy oral consumer - that pattern, not the raw case count, is what independently_replicated:yes and consistency:consistent are tracking here.
claims.notes: Related but not pooled into this row: PROSPECT (a large ICU RCT, see imm-vap in immune.json) found L. rhamnosus recovered from a normally sterile site in 15/1318 (1.1%) probiotic-group ICU patients vs 1/1332 (0.1%) controls - a sterile-site-culture signal in critically ill adults, not a bacteremia case series, but consistent with the same compromised-barrier risk pattern. A single-center NICU cohort also found higher necrotizing enterocolitis incidence after routine LGG adoption (see gi-nec-prevention) - NEC itself is a different outcome from bacteremia, but the two safety signals co-occur in the same preterm population and both argue for caution in NICU use specifically. Several additional L. rhamnosus bacteremia case reports exist in the literature (renal transplant, burn patient, recurrent bacteremia/endocarditis, splenic hematoma) but were excluded here because the reports available did not confirm strain GG specifically versus another L. rhamnosus strain or an unidentified commercial product - per the taxonomy trap discipline, species-level 'L. rhamnosus' case reports are not treated as GG-specific evidence.

gaps: No formal incidence rate (cases per million doses sold) was found to contextualize how rare bacteremia/fungemia events are against GG's very high global consumption volume - the case-report literature by its nature cannot supply a denominator, which is exactly why it caps at tier D rather than being read as a meaningful population-level risk estimate.
